analysis.one_liner: Lets people exposed to toxic PFAS chemicals sue manufacturers and shift medical monitoring costs to them.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 4 House Democrats, never received a committee vote or a floor vote and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: PFAS are 'forever chemicals' used in manufacturing that build up in human blood and have been linked to cancer and other chronic diseases. This bill would write into federal law a right to sue any company that made or helped make the PFAS you were exposed to, and would make those companies pay for ongoing medical monitoring — periodic checkups to catch PFAS-linked diseases early. It also would let courts lower the usual scientific proof standard when safety research is thin, and order companies to fund the missing studies.
analysis.who_benefits: People with significant PFAS exposure — from contaminated drinking water, work sites, or communities near manufacturing plants — gain a federal lawsuit right that does not currently exist, plus a court-ordered medical monitoring remedy paid for by the responsible companies, not the exposed individuals.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a federal cause of action allowing individuals significantly exposed to PFAS — individually or as a class — to sue any person that engaged in any portion of the manufacturing process that created the PFAS and foresaw or should have foresee human exposure [S2].

Codifies medical monitoring as a remedy: courts may award periodic diagnostic examinations when exposure raises the risk of a PFAS-associated disease, shifting those costs from exposed individuals to the responsible parties [S2].

Sets a presumption of significant exposure when a defendant's PFAS was released into an area where a person lived or worked for at least a year, or when blood testing detects PFAS in a person's body [S2].

Lets courts lower the standard of scientific proof for disease risk when independent toxicological data does not yet exist, and order new epidemiological or toxicological studies as part of the remedy [S2].

The bill's findings note PFAS have been detected in the drinking water of at least 200,000,000 people in the U.S. and are linked to cancer, reproductive and developmental harm, and immune-system harm [S2].

analysis.who_pays: PFAS manufacturers and any company in their production chain — including toll manufacturers and fluorosurfactant users — would face federal lawsuits, medical monitoring awards, and court-ordered research costs, and would bear the cost of rebuttal blood testing.
analysis.who_pays_short: PFAS makers and their supply chains

drawbacks.text: Liability is broad: any company that engaged in 'any portion' of a manufacturing process creating the PFAS can be sued, which could sweep in businesses far down the chemical supply chain that merely used PFAS in their own production [S2].

When the science is incomplete, courts may lower the standard of proof for disease risk, meaning claims could succeed on evidence that would not meet the usual scientific bar — a real due-process concern for defendants and a reason outcomes could rest on thin data [S2].

A presumption of exposure triggered by one year in an affected area, rebuttable only through independent testing the defendant must pay for, tilts the litigation framework toward plaintiffs and could generate large settlement costs that companies may pass to consumers [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people carrying PFAS in their blood — with no natural source and links to serious disease — the bill offers something that does not otherwise exist: a federal way to get medical checkups paid for by the companies that made the chemicals. The cost lands on chemical makers and their customers, and the framework (broad producer liability, plaintiff-friendly presumptions, lowered proof standards) is written to favor exposed individuals. Critics could fairly call the evidentiary shortcuts excessive, but the bill does not preempt state law claims or create an exclusive remedy, leaving ordinary court routes intact [S2].

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees the day it was introduced, one sent it to a subcommittee, and neither committee ever voted it out — so it never reached the House floor, and it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Madeleine Dean of Pennsylvania introduced the PFAS Accountability Act of 2024 in the House on February 1, 2024, joined by Reps. Nadler and Kildee [S2][S4].
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Judiciary Committee on the day of introduction [S4].

The next day it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Environment, Manufacturing, and Critical Materials; the action history shows no hearings, markup, or floor vote ever followed [S4].
The bill drew 3 cosponsors, all Democrats [S3].
The bill's findings state that before its enactment no federal statutory cause of action existed for individuals harmed by long-term PFAS exposure [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: PFAS manufacturers and companies in their supply chains are better off: they avoid a federal lawsuit right with plaintiff-friendly exposure presumptions and court-ordered medical monitoring and research costs. People exposed to PFAS remain without the federal cause of action the bill would have created [S2][S4].

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: PFAS manufacturers and their supply chains

for.name: Madeleine Dean
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 1, 2024, creating a federal cause of action and medical monitoring remedy for people significantly exposed to PFAS.

for.name: Jerry Nadler
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor whose Judiciary Committee jurisdiction covered the cause-of-action provision; the bill was jointly referred to his committee.

for.name: Dan Kildee
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor; his Michigan district includes PFAS-affected communities.

for.name: Frank Pallone
for.role: Ranking Member, House Energy and Commerce
for.what_they_did: Home-state? No — senior environmental-policy Democrat on the committee the bill was referred to; supported PFAS accountability measures in the 118th Congress.

against.name: Cathy McMorris Rodgers
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Her committee received the bill on February 1, 2024 and referred it to a subcommittee the next day; no markup or vote was ever scheduled, and the bill died there.

against.name: Jim Jordan
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill the day it was introduced and took no further action on it before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 3 cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican signed on; the Republican chairs of both committees to which the bill was referred never scheduled any action on it [S3][S4].

industries.note: The bill exposes companies that make PFAS to federal lawsuits from anyone significantly exposed, with a presumption of exposure after a year in an affected area or a positive blood test, plus court-ordered medical monitoring and research costs. For the public, that shifts the price of contamination-related health monitoring onto the companies that made the chemicals.

industries.industry: Manufacturers that use PFAS in their own production (toll manufacturers, fluorosurfactant users)
industries.note: Liability reaches 'any portion of a manufacturing process that created the PFAS,' so companies beyond the original chemical maker can be sued. These firms have resisted PFAS liability broadly in Congress and the courts.

industries.industry: Independent medical testing and toxicology providers
industries.note: The bill requires court-ordered diagnostic monitoring and defendant-funded independent blood testing to rebut exposure presumptions, creating paid work for testing labs and clinicians. The benefit runs alongside the public's interest in early disease detection.
